title: Who Belongs and How to Live
overview: A collection of laws about who could join Israel's gathered community and how to keep its camp, worship, money, promises and fields clean and fair.

parts.label: Limits on joining (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: Men with damaged genitals and children of marriages the law forbade, probably incestuous ones, were kept out of "the assembly of the LORD," meaning the people gathered as God's community. The prophet Isaiah later promises eunuchs and foreigners who hold to God a lasting place among God's people (Isaiah 56).

parts.label: Neighbors judged by history (vv. 3-8)
parts.note: Ammon and Moab were barred, with "ten generations" probably meaning never, because they did not come out to meet Israel with bread and water on the journey and they hired the seer Balaam to curse Israel. Edom, descended from Jacob's brother Esau, and Egypt, where Israel once lived as guests, were treated more warmly, and their grandchildren could fully join.

parts.label: A clean army camp (vv. 9-14)
parts.note: A soldier with a nighttime emission counted as ritually unclean and stayed outside the camp until he washed at evening, and everyone dug and covered their waste outside the camp. The reason given is that God moved among them, so the camp had to be fit for that presence, and it was sound hygiene too.

parts.label: Refuge for runaway slaves (vv. 15-16)
parts.note: A slave who escaped to Israel was not to be sent back but could settle in any town they chose, free from mistreatment. This stands out, since other ancient law codes required runaways to be returned, though it is unclear whether it covered slaves of Israelite masters or only foreign ones.

parts.label: Prostitution and the temple (vv. 17-18)
parts.note: The words used are related to "holy" and are often taken to mean sex tied to shrine worship, though scholars debate how common that really was. Money earned by any prostitute, female or male (the "dog" of some translations), could not be given to God to pay a vow.

parts.label: Loans, vows and fields (vv. 19-25)
parts.note: Israelites were not to charge each other interest, since loans usually helped a neighbor in need, though they could charge foreigners, who often borrowed for trade. Vows to God were optional but binding once spoken, and a hungry passerby could eat from a neighbor's vines or grain but not carry any away.

disagreement: Interpreters differ on what being kept out of "the assembly of the LORD" actually meant, whether exclusion from worship, from leadership, or from marrying into Israel, and so on how harsh these limits really were.
think: When a community draws lines about who fully belongs, what makes a line seem fair or unfair to you?
